title: Leadership Samuel D. James An Ounce of Clarity vs a Pound of Cleverness
author: James, Samuel D.
summary: James argues, through the comparison of two books he reads simultaneously -- a plain pastor's book and a clever but meandering career writer's book -- that clarity in communication is worth more than cleverness. The central diagnostic is that authors reach most desperately for cleverness when they don't know what they're trying to say: cleverness functions like nervous laughter, filling silence for the writer while distracting the reader. James connects clarity to usefulness: clear writing gives people ideas that stick, arguments that can be used in day-to-day thinking, concepts that illuminate subsequent learning -- while clever writing impresses briefly and is forgotten quickly. The article also argues that clarity is the structural virtue that makes other literary flaws more forgivable: when a reader grasps what the writer means, generalisations and oversights are less damaging than when the central point is opaque. The piece is a call for communicators and leaders to subordinate style to substance, understanding that the benefits of cleverness are short-lived while the benefits of clarity tend to compound.
points: * Authors reach most desperately for cleverness when they don't know what they're trying to say: cleverness functions like nervous laughter -- filling silence for the one providing it, distracting for everyone else, masking the absence of argument. * Clarity is the structural virtue that makes other writing flaws more forgivable: when a reader grasps the point, oversweeping generalisations are manageable; when clarity is absent, every flaw is amplified and the reader loses trust. * The benefits of cleverness are short-lived -- readers are impressed briefly then move on -- while the benefits of clarity tend to reproduce and compound: clear ideas reappear in the reader's thinking and are quoted reflexively by other writers. * Lack of clarity is like pride: a literary sin in itself that also makes every other sin worse -- logical errors, off-putting style, and unanswered objections all become more damaging when the central argument cannot be confidently grasped. * Writing that helps tends to keep on helping: a concept explained clearly leads to other concepts understood better, and this compounding usefulness separates writing to remember from writing to skim.
quotes: In writing, an ounce of clarity is worth more than a pound of cleverness.
When I spend time in the pastor's book, I know what he's saying. His language is not impressive, but it's clear, and it's convincing. He has a message and he executes it.

If love covers a multitude of real sins, clarity covers a multitude of literary ones. The pastor's book has some flaws -- intuitive objections get overlooked rather than engaged, and sometimes the generalizations are too sweeping. But the clarity of thought dilutes the impact of these flaws.

Authors tend to reach more desperately for cleverness when they don't know what they're trying to say. A lot of cleverness in writing functions like nervous laughter in conversation. It fills silence for the one providing it, but it's distracting for everyone else.
Lack of clarity is like pride: it's a literary sin in itself, but it also makes other literary sins worse.

People who are impressed by cleverness don't stay impressed very long. Most readers think of clever writing the way people think of big, rich yards. When you see it for the first time, you think, 'Wow, that's a beautiful yard.' When you see it for the third time, you think, 'Man, I would hate to mow all this.'
Clarity is the kind of skill that separates writing to skim from writing to remember.
